1.q: A practice nurse is planning activities for a GP surgery's prevention week. Which activity is an example of primary prevention?
o: Giving the MMRV vaccine to a child at her one-year appointment
Offering cervical screening to a 30-year-old woman
Sending a bowel screening kit to a 62-year-old man
Referring a man to cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
1.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: primary prevention is prevention of disease through control of exposure to risk factors. Immunisation prevents infection before it occurs (UKHSA routine schedule from 1 September 2026: MMRV at one year).

n.1: Screening detects early departures from health in people who already have changes, so it is secondary prevention.
n.2: Bowel screening aims to find cancer or polyps early, which is secondary prevention.
n.3: Rehabilitation reduces impairment from existing disease, so it is tertiary prevention.

1.q: Amira, 45, has pneumonia. On assessment her airway is clear. Her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and SpO2 is 89% on air. She has no history of lung disease. According to the ABCDE approach, what should you do next?
o: Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 88-92% and summon help
Move straight on to assess her pulse, blood pressure and capillary refill
Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 94-98% and summon help
Ask her to take deep breaths and recheck her saturation in an hour
1.w: Problems found under B are treated before moving to C. For acutely ill adults not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure the target is 94-98% (BTS; NICE NG253 rec 1.10.1), so start oxygen and get help early.

n.0: 88-92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, which Amira is not.
n.1: ABCDE requires treating the breathing problem found at B before assessing circulation.
n.3: An hour's delay with SpO2 89% and RR 28 leaves hypoxaemia untreated.

1.q: Amara is a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward in England. During induction a colleague explains that one organisation sets the professional standards in the Code and can take action if a registrant's fitness to practise is impaired. Which organisation is the colleague describing?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Royal College of Nursing
The Care Quality Commission
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
1.w: The NMC is the professional regulator for nurses, midwives and nursing associates: it publishes the Code (2015, updated 2018), keeps the register and deals with fitness to practise concerns about individual registrants.

n.1: The RCN is a professional body and trade union; it supports nurses but has no regulatory powers over registration.
n.2: The CQC regulates registered providers of health and social care in England (for example enforcing regulation 20, the statutory duty of candour), not individual nurses.
n.3: NICE produces evidence-based guidance; it does not register nurses or judge fitness to practise.

1.q: During an ABCDE assessment of Jordan, 30, who was admitted with a gastrointestinal bleed, you note a pulse of 124 beats per minute, BP 92/60 mmHg, cool peripheries and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which assessment step are these findings part of?
o: Breathing
Circulation
Exposure
Disability
1.w: Pulse, blood pressure, peripheral temperature and capillary refill time are all assessed under C (circulation). These findings suggest hypovolaemia and need urgent escalation (NICE CG174 lists HR over 90, systolic under 100 and CRT over 2 seconds as indicators for urgent fluid resuscitation).

n.0: Breathing covers respiratory rate, effort, oxygen saturation and chest sounds, not perfusion.
n.2: Exposure covers full skin examination, temperature, wounds, drains and bleeding sites.
n.3: Disability covers level of consciousness, pupils and blood glucose.

1.q: Section 47 enquiries are started at a strategy discussion about Mason, 2, who has a femoral fracture with no explanation. The health visitor asks when an initial child protection conference should take place if concerns are substantiated. What timescale does Working Together 2026 set?
o: Within 10 working days of the strategy discussion
Within 5 working days of the strategy discussion
Within 45 working days of the original referral
Within 15 working days of the strategy discussion
1.w: Working Together 2026 sets the initial child protection conference within 15 working days of the strategy discussion, or of the last strategy discussion if more than one was held, at which s47 enquiries were initiated.

n.0: Ten working days is the timescale for the first core group meeting after the initial conference.
n.1: Five working days is too short and is not the conference timescale.
n.2: 45 working days is the maximum for completing an assessment, not for convening the conference.

1.q: Nurse Ola is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Mr Grant, 55, who is alert. Which question type is most appropriate immediately before giving the first dose?
o: An open question about how he feels about his treatment
A reflective question about his previous hospital stays
A closed question confirming any penicillin allergy
A leading question assuming that he has no allergies
1.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questions. Closed questions obtain specific facts, such as allergy status, quickly and clearly; Code 18 safe medicines practice.

n.0: Open questions are useful for exploring feelings but not for confirming a specific safety fact.
n.1: This does not establish the specific allergy information needed now.
n.3: Leading questions can produce a false answer to a safety-critical check.

1.q: On a medical ward in England, Mr Hughes, 70, was given a tenfold insulin overdose and needed transfer to intensive care. The ward manager asks which organisation regulates the trust's compliance with the statutory duty of candour under regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations. Which organisation is this?
o: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Health and Safety Executive
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
1.w: The statutory duty of candour (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, reg 20) applies to registered providers and is regulated by the CQC in England. The professional duty in Code 14 is overseen by the NMC for individual registrants.

n.1: The NMC oversees the professional duty of candour of individual registrants (Code 14), not the provider's statutory duty under reg 20.
n.2: The HSE enforces workplace health and safety law such as HASAWA 1974 and RIDDOR, not reg 20 of the 2014 Regulations.
n.3: The Ombudsman investigates unresolved complaints about the NHS; it does not regulate providers' compliance with reg 20.

1.q: Tom, aged 18 months, attends clinic with his father. He walks independently, scribbles with a crayon, points to show things he wants and uses about five single words. His father asks whether Tom should be joining words together yet. What is the best reply?
o: He should be speaking in short sentences of three or four words by now
Two-word phrases usually appear around 2 years, so his speech is on track
Single words are expected by 2 years, so he is ahead of his age
Two-word phrases usually appear by 12 months, so he needs a speech referral
1.w: At 18 months children typically use several single words and follow simple instructions; combining two words ('more milk') is expected around 2 years (CDC 2022 milestones). Tom's language and other skills fit his age, so the nurse can reassure his father and explain what to expect next.

n.0: Three- to four-word sentences belong to around 3 years, not 18 months.
n.2: Single words are expected well before 2 years (around 12 to 18 months), so Tom is on track rather than ahead.
n.3: Two-word phrases are not expected at 12 months, when a child typically says 'mama' or 'dada'.

1.q: Nurse Jo has taught Mrs Akhtar, 70, how to use a new inhaler. Which approach best checks that Mrs Akhtar has understood?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to read it tonight
Ask her whether she understands how to use the inhaler
Ask her to show how she will use the inhaler at home
Repeat the explanation slowly a second time
1.w: Annexe A 1.6: check understanding and use clarification techniques. Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum.

n.0: A leaflet supports learning but does not check understanding now.
n.1: A yes or no answer does not show whether she can use it correctly.
n.3: Repetition may help, but it does not check what she has understood.

1.q: Doris, 76, is unconscious after a stroke and needs her bed linen changed. Two staff are available. Which technique is most appropriate?
o: Roll her to each side in turn, changing half the sheet each time
Lift her out to a chair while the bed is stripped and remade
Change the top sheet and add an extra pad underneath her
Leave the soiled sheet until she regains consciousness
1.w: Annexe B 3.2: bed-making for an unconscious or immobile person is done with the person in the bed, rolling them to each side with enough staff and appropriate handling aids, keeping the airway clear and maintaining dignity.

n.1: Transferring an unconscious person to a chair is unsafe and unnecessary.
n.2: Adding pads over soiled linen leaves her lying on moisture and risks pressure damage.
n.3: Leaving soiled linen risks skin damage and infection and is undignified.

1.q: Baby Grace, born at term, is admitted to a children's ward at 2 days old for observation. Her axillary temperature is 36.0°C. She is alert, pink and feeding well, and her mother is with her. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Undress her under a fan heater directed at the cot
Place a hot water bottle in the cot beside her
Bath her in warm water to raise her temperature quickly
Skin-to-skin with her mother in a warm, draught-free room
1.w: Thermoregulation in newborns (BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice point 8; neonatal care principles): newborns lose heat quickly by evaporation, conduction, convection and radiation. Dry the baby, use a hat, place skin-to-skin with the parent and keep the room warm and draught-free, then recheck temperature.

n.0: Undressing increases heat loss, and a directed fan heater risks burns and convective loss.
n.1: Hot water bottles risk burns and are not used to warm newborns.
n.2: Bathing increases evaporative heat loss once the baby is out of the water.

1.q: Doreen, 79, is fluid overloaded with worsening breathlessness. The registrar, who is scrubbed in theatre for the next 2 hours, phones the ward to add a single dose of intravenous furosemide now. Trust policy permits verbal orders in exceptional circumstances. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Accept it per policy and ask for written confirmation within 7 days
Refuse, and wait for the registrar to write it after theatre
Write the new dose on the drug chart herself and sign it as the prescriber
Accept it per policy and ensure written confirmation, ideally within 24 hours
1.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20: in exceptional circumstances, where delay would compromise care and the medicine is not a Schedule 2 CD, verbal orders may be used under organisational policy; the prescriber then amends the chart or provides a prescription as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

n.0: The RPS/RCN standard is ideally within 24 hours, not 7 days.
n.1: A 2-hour delay could compromise Doreen's care when policy allows a verbal order.
n.2: Transcribing cannot be used to add a new medicine; the nurse would be acting as an unauthorised prescriber.

1.q: Mr Achebe, 62, is admitted to a medical ward with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The nurse is starting his admission assessment and wants it to be person-centred and shared. Which opening approach best achieves this?
o: Ask his wife to describe his usual routine and difficulties
Review his medical notes and set goals for him to work on
Ask what matters most to him and what he hopes to achieve
Complete the trust checklist, then explain the plan to him
1.w: NMC proficiency P3.4 requires a person-centred approach with shared assessment, planning, decision-making and goal setting; Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with the person. Starting with what matters to Mr Achebe puts him at the centre of the assessment.

n.0: His wife may add useful information, but he can speak for himself and should be asked first.
n.1: Setting goals for him rather than with him is not shared goal setting.
n.3: Completing a checklist first and then informing him is not shared assessment or decision-making.

1.q: Sunita, 52, feels well and has no symptoms. After receiving an NHS invitation letter, she attends her GP surgery for cervical screening, and the practice nurse takes a sample. Which level of prevention does this activity represent?
o: Secondary prevention
Health protection
Primary prevention
Tertiary prevention
1.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: secondary prevention is the application of available measures to detect early departures from health and to introduce appropriate treatment; screening, such as cervical screening, is a major component.

n.1: Health protection covers measures such as infection control and immunisation, not detecting early disease in individuals.
n.2: Primary prevention controls exposure to risk factors before disease starts, for example immunisation or stopping smoking.
n.3: Tertiary prevention reduces long-term impairment and disability from established disease, such as rehabilitation.

1.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
1.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

1.q: You are caring for Harold, 78, who is in a side room with confirmed Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea. You have just helped him to the commode and removed your gloves and apron. What is the most appropriate method of hand hygiene now?
o: Apply alcohol-based handrub, rubbing all surfaces for 20 to 30 seconds
Use a detergent hand wipe, then apply alcohol-based handrub
Rub hands with an antimicrobial surgical scrub solution until dry
Wash with liquid soap and running water, then dry with paper towels
1.w: NHS England NIPCM (ch 1.2) says wash hands with non-antimicrobial liquid soap and water when caring for a patient with a suspected or known gastrointestinal infection, such as a spore-forming organism like C. difficile. Alcohol does not reliably act against spores, so mechanical removal by washing is needed.

n.0: Alcohol-based handrub is the routine method, but it is not effective against C. difficile spores, so NIPCM directs soap and water here.
n.1: Hand wipes followed by handrub are a fallback for when running water is unavailable; Harold's side room has running water.
n.2: Surgical scrub products are for surgical hand antisepsis before sterile procedures, not routine care of a patient with C. difficile.

1.q: Mr Okafor, 68, is recovering from a hip replacement and has capacity. After the nurse explains why his evening enoxaparin injection is prescribed and the risk of a blood clot, he says clearly that he does not want it tonight. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Respect his decision, document the refusal and inform the prescriber
Carry out a formal mental capacity assessment before accepting the refusal
Record the omission code on the chart and review at tomorrow's dose
Ask his daughter to visit and persuade him to accept the injection
1.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment; Code 4.1 balances best interests with that right. Informing the prescriber allows the VTE plan to be reviewed (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.1: Capacity is presumed (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and nothing suggests he lacks it; refusing advice is not itself evidence of incapacity.
n.2: Recording the code is part of the answer, but the prescriber must be told so the VTE risk can be reviewed now.
n.3: Recruiting family to pressure him undermines his autonomy; Code 2.5 requires the nurse to respect and support his right to refuse.

1.q: Baby Zainab was born at 39 weeks and is 18 hours old on the postnatal ward. During a feed her mother notices her skin and eyes look yellow. The nurse confirms visible jaundice. What should happen next?
o: Serum bilirubin measured within 6 hours if still yellow
Reassurance that this is normal physiological jaundice
Transcutaneous bilirubin measured at the 24-hour check
Serum bilirubin measured within 2 hours and medical review
1.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023) recs 1.2.10-1.2.12: jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proved otherwise; measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours) and arrange urgent medical review (within 6 hours). Serum, not transcutaneous, measurement is used in the first 24 hours.

n.0: Within 6 hours is the timeframe for babies more than 24 hours old; Zainab is 18 hours old.
n.1: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is not physiological; it may signal haemolysis or infection.
n.2: Transcutaneous measurement is not used in the first 24 hours (rec 1.2.15), and waiting delays an urgent test.

1.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
1.q: A nurse needs to record the respiratory rate of Leo, a 4-month-old baby who is asleep in his cot. Which technique is most accurate?
o: Count for 15 seconds and multiply the number by four
Count while he is asleep, watching the abdomen for 60 seconds
Wake him gently first so his chest movements are clearer
Use the reading displayed on the pulse oximeter instead
1.w: Infants breathe mainly with the diaphragm and often irregularly, so the respiratory rate should be counted for a full 60 seconds by watching the abdomen, ideally before disturbing the baby, as crying and handling raise the rate (AnnexB.2.1: observations; P3.12).

n.0: Irregular infant breathing makes short counts inaccurate.
n.2: Waking him causes crying and raises the rate, giving a falsely high reading.
n.3: A pulse oximeter measures saturation and pulse, not respiratory rate.

1.q: A healthcare assistant asks Sofia, a staff nurse, what the Code means by 'the fundamentals of care' that every registrant must deliver effectively (standard 1.2). Which aspect of care does the Code name as one of the fundamentals?
o: Discharge planning with the wider team
Medicines reconciliation on admission
Wound assessment and dressing selection
Bladder and bowel care
1.w: The note to Code 1.2 says the fundamentals of care include, but are not limited to, nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and keeping people in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Discharge planning relates to coordinating care, not to the fundamentals listed in the note to standard 1.2.
n.1: Medicines reconciliation is important but it falls under standard 18 on medicines, not the Code's definition of fundamentals of care.
n.2: Wound care is a clinical procedure; the Code's fundamentals are nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and hygiene.

1.q: A mother tells a nurse on a children's ward that she saw a healthcare assistant roughly grab her son's arm and swear at him during the night. The healthcare assistant is still on shift. Under Working Together 2026, what should happen to this allegation?
o: It is recorded in the incident system and reviewed at the next team meeting
Report it to a senior manager now; the LADO is told within one working day
The nurse discusses it with the healthcare assistant before deciding to report
It is reported to the NMC, which will decide whether the LADO needs to be involved
1.w: Working Together 2026 (para 264) says any allegation against a person who works with children should be reported immediately to a senior manager, and the Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO) should be informed within one working day. Immediate action to protect the child, such as removing the staff member from contact, is also needed.

n.0: Waiting for a team meeting delays protection and the required report to the LADO.
n.2: Discussing the allegation with the person concerned first may compromise any investigation and leaves the child at risk.
n.3: The NMC does not regulate healthcare assistants, and the LADO advises on regulator referrals, not the other way round.

1.q: Joseph, a staff nurse, is reviewing a NICE guideline with a student nurse. The student asks what legal status NICE guidance has for registered nurses caring for an individual patient. Which statement by Joseph is most accurate?
o: It replaces individual clinical judgement whenever a recommendation applies
It should be taken fully into account alongside the person's needs and preferences
It carries the same legal force as an Act of Parliament once it is published
It applies to medical staff, while nurses follow local trust policy instead
1.w: NICE's standard 'Your responsibility' statement (seen in NG253) says guidance is not mandatory: professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside the individual needs, preferences and values of the person. Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based.

n.0: NICE states its guidance supports, and does not replace, the professional's judgement about the individual person.
n.2: NICE guidance is not legislation; it does not have the force of an Act of Parliament.
n.3: NICE guidance applies to all health professionals, including nurses, not to medical staff alone.

1.q: According to the NMC Code (2018), which of the following is listed among the fundamentals of care that nurses must deliver?
o: Medicines reconciliation
Discharge planning
Health education
Bladder and bowel care
1.w: Code 1.2 (NMC 2018): fundamentals of care include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and making sure people are kept in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Medicines reconciliation is not one of the Code's listed fundamentals.
n.1: Discharge planning is important but is not in the Code's list of fundamentals.
n.2: Health education is not in the Code's list of fundamentals of care.

1.q: Ella, 9 months, is choking on a piece of apple in a clinic waiting room. She is conscious, but her cough is now silent and she cannot cry. Help has been called. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give up to 5 back blows with Ella head-down along the forearm
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts with Ella held upright
Sweep a finger through Ella's mouth to hook out the food
Give 5 rescue breaths with Ella lying flat on her back
1.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support choking algorithm: if the cough becomes ineffective in a conscious infant, give up to 5 back blows with the infant face down along the forearm and head lower than the chest, then up to 5 chest thrusts.

n.1: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of abdominal organ injury; infants receive chest thrusts after back blows.
n.2: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further down; remove it only if clearly visible.
n.3: Rescue breaths start when a choking child becomes unconscious; Ella is still conscious.

1.q: Arthur, 82, is in a four-bed bay and needs help to use a commode. The curtains around his bed space do not fully close and a visitor is sitting at the next bed. Which action best protects his privacy and dignity?
o: Help him quickly so that he is exposed for as short a time as possible
Delay the commode until visiting time has finished in an hour
Ask the visitor to look away while you help him onto the commode
Close the gap with a dignity clip and tell him before starting
1.w: Annexe B 3.4 requires privacy and dignity at all times, and Code 1.1 requires dignity in all care. Secure the screens fully (for example with dignity clips) and explain what you are doing before starting personal care.

n.0: Speed reduces exposure but leaves him visible through the gap.
n.1: Delaying elimination is uncomfortable, undignified and risks incontinence.
n.2: Relying on a visitor to look away does not provide privacy.

1.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
1.q: Maisie, 2 years old, is admitted for observation after a minor head injury. She is playing calmly. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and heart rate 120 beats/min. How should the nurse interpret these values?
o: The breathing rate is raised but the heart rate is normal
Both are within the normal range for her age
The heart rate is raised but the breathing rate is normal
Both are raised and need escalation for review
1.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1, approximate normal ranges): at 2 years, respiratory rate 18 to 40 breaths/min and heart rate 90 to 160 beats/min. A rate of 30 and heart rate of 120 in a calm toddler are normal (T2 vital signs by age).

n.0: A respiratory rate of 30 is within the 18 to 40 range at 2 years.
n.2: A heart rate of 120 is well within the 90 to 160 range at 2 years.
n.3: Neither value is above the upper limit for a 2-year-old, so escalation for these values is not needed.

1.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
1.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

1.q: Chloe, a registered nurse in a sexual health clinic, sees Zara, 22, who requests emergency hormonal contraception. No prescriber is on site. The clinic has an authorised written direction covering this medicine for defined groups of patients. Under which mechanism can Chloe supply it?
o: A verbal order from an on-call doctor
A homely remedy protocol
A patient specific direction
A patient group direction
1.w: A patient group direction (PGD) is a written direction allowing named, authorised registered professionals such as nurses to supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group of patients without an individual prescription (MHRA; Human Medicines Regulations 2012).

n.0: Verbal orders are for exceptional changes to existing administration details, not first supply to a new patient.
n.1: Homely remedy protocols cover non-POM medicines in settings such as care homes, not this clinic's POM supply.
n.2: A PSD is an instruction from a prescriber for a named patient after individual assessment; no prescriber has assessed Zara.

1.q: Mrs Fisher, 89, is frail and lives in a care home. Staff report she has become drowsy and less able to feed herself since yesterday. Her temperature is 36.4°C and her urine is cloudy. A colleague says infection is unlikely because she has no fever. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that frail older people may have infection without fever
Ask the care home to collect a urine sample at the next GP visit
Agree, and look for a non-infective cause of her new drowsiness
Agree, and plan to recheck her temperature again in 4 hours
1.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever or hypothermia alone to rule sepsis in or out; rec 1.4.2 notes older or very frail people may not develop a raised temperature, and rec 1.4.9 that cognitive change may present as acute change in function. She needs full assessment and NEWS2.

n.1: Deferring a sample delays assessment of an acute change in an older, frail person.
n.2: Excluding infection on the basis of a normal temperature contradicts NG253 rec 1.4.1.
n.3: Waiting 4 hours for a temperature ignores signs of possible sepsis that need assessment now.

1.q: George, 86, has end-stage heart failure and lives in a nursing home. Over two days he has become harder to rouse, has stopped eating, and his knees look mottled. His breathing alternates between deep breaths and pauses. Which group of findings most suggests that George may be entering the last days of life?
o: Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and increasing peripheral oedema
New fever, a productive cough and a respiratory rate of 26 per minute
Improved alertness, taking more fluids and fewer respiratory secretions
Mottled skin, Cheyne-Stokes breathing and a falling level of consciousness
1.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.2 lists signs that may suggest a person is entering the last days of life: agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, deteriorating level of consciousness, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions and progressive weight loss, alongside increasing fatigue, loss of appetite and functional decline.

n.0: These suggest fluid overload or worsening heart failure, not the recognised signs that a person may be dying.
n.1: These findings point to a possible chest infection or sepsis that needs assessment and escalation; they are not the NG31 signs of dying.
n.2: NICE NG31 1.1.3 says improvement in signs, symptoms or function may mean the person is stabilising or recovering.

1.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
1.q: Jayden, aged 6, has a blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg on the ward. The nurse notices the cuff covers only half the length of his upper arm. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the reading and inform the doctor of hypertension
Record the reading and repeat it in 4 hours
Repeat the reading with the same cuff on the other arm
Repeat the reading with a correctly sized cuff
1.w: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high blood pressure reading. The cuff must be the correct size for the child's arm before a reading is interpreted, so the reading should be repeated with an appropriately sized cuff (AnnexB.2.1: taking blood pressure manually and via electronic devices).

n.0: The reading is unreliable because of the cuff size, so it should not yet be reported as hypertension.
n.1: Recording a reading taken with the wrong cuff puts inaccurate data on the chart.
n.2: Using the same small cuff on the other arm repeats the same error.

1.q: Graham, 54, has a BMI of 34 and is at a health check. The nurse explains the health risks of his weight and the support available. Graham says he does not want to change his diet at the moment because of stress at work. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell him he must start changing his diet now to avoid a heart attack
Record that he is non-compliant and close the health promotion episode
Refer him to a weight management service even though he has declined
Respect his decision, give information and offer to revisit the topic later
1.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.1 and P2.9: promote health by empowering people to make informed choices, using communication skills and strength-based approaches. NICE PH49 (2014) recommends tailoring interventions to the person's motivation and planning review points; Code 4.1 respects the person's right to accept or refuse.

n.0: Pressuring or frightening him is not empowering; NMC P2.1 and P2.9 support informed choices.
n.1: Labelling him non-compliant is judgemental and closes the door on future support.
n.2: Referral needs his agreement; acting against his choice undermines informed decision-making (Code 4).

1.q: Nurse Leon is admitting Mrs Clarke, 63, after a bowel resection. He wants to encourage her to describe her recovery in her own words. Which question is most appropriate?
o: "Are you feeling better than yesterday?"
"Have you had any pain since your operation?"
"You're managing well with the pain now, aren't you?"
"How have you been feeling since your operation?"
1.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questioning. Open questions invite the person to describe their experience in their own words; Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This closed question limits her to a comparison and a short answer.
n.1: This is a closed question that invites a yes or no answer.
n.2: This is a leading question that suggests the answer she should give.

1.q: A family court in England is deciding where Ruby, 6, should live after her parents separate. The children's nurse who has cared for Ruby during a long admission is asked to provide a statement and wants to understand the principle the court must apply. Which principle governs the court's decision?
o: The rights of each parent are weighed equally with Ruby's welfare
The wishes of the parent who has day-to-day care decide the outcome
Ruby's best interests are a primary consideration among several
Ruby's welfare is the court's paramount consideration
1.w: The Children Act 1989 s1(1) states that when a court determines any question about a child's upbringing, the child's welfare shall be the court's paramount consideration (the paramountcy principle).

n.0: Parental rights are not balanced equally against the child's welfare; welfare is paramount under s1(1).
n.1: The resident parent's wishes are one factor the court may consider, not the deciding test.
n.2: 'A primary consideration' is the UNCRC Article 3 wording; the domestic court test under s1(1) is stronger, making welfare paramount.

1.q: Noah, 6, collapses on a children's ward and is not breathing. Two registered nurses trained in paediatric basic life support start resuscitation after the initial rescue breaths. What ratio of compressions to ventilations should they use?
o: 5 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
3 compressions to 1 breath
1.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: rescuers trained in paediatric BLS use 15:2 for infants and children, in and out of hospital. 30:2 is for untrained or adult-trained bystanders.

n.0: 5:1 is an outdated ratio that is not part of current RCUK paediatric guidance.
n.2: 30:2 is advised for rescuers not trained in paediatric BLS; trained ward nurses use 15:2.
n.3: 3:1 is the newborn life support ratio at birth, not the ratio for a 6-year-old.

1.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
1.q: Ben, aged 10, is resting in bed with a chest infection. His heart rate is 150 beats/min and respiratory rate 32 breaths/min. He is afebrile. What does this indicate?
o: Normal values, because children have faster rates than adults
A raised heart rate but normal breathing for a 10-year-old
Both values are above the normal range for his age
A normal heart rate but rapid breathing for a 10-year-old
1.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1): at 10 years, the approximate normal respiratory rate is 14 to 25 breaths/min and heart rate 60 to 120 beats/min. Both values are well above the upper limit at rest without fever, so the nurse should assess further and escalate.

n.0: Rates are faster in children, but a resting heart rate of 150 and breathing rate of 32 exceed the range at 10 years.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 32 is above the upper limit of about 25 at 10 years.
n.3: A heart rate of 150 is above the upper limit of about 120 at 10 years.

2.q: Leo was born at 40 weeks and is now 16 days old. He is breastfed and still looks jaundiced. His mother says his stools have become pale and chalky and his urine darkens the nappy. What should the health visitor do?
o: Arrange same-day medical assessment, including conjugated bilirubin
Reassure her that breast milk jaundice can last up to 12 weeks
Advise stopping breastfeeding for 48 hours to see if it fades
Advise placing Leo near a sunny window for short periods
2.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023) rec 1.7.1: jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby (21 days if preterm) needs assessment for pale chalky stools and dark urine, and measurement of conjugated bilirubin. Pale stools and dark urine suggest conjugated jaundice such as biliary atresia, which needs urgent specialist referral.

n.1: Breast milk jaundice does not cause pale stools and dark urine; these suggest liver disease.
n.2: CG98 advises that breastfeeding can usually continue; stopping it does not investigate the cause.
n.3: CG98 says do not use sunlight as treatment for jaundice.

2.q: Following a referral about Josh, 8, who disclosed that his father burned him with a cigarette, the local authority holds a strategy discussion because there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm. Under Working Together 2026, which agencies must, as a minimum, be involved?
o: Police, health and the Local Authority Designated Officer
Children's social care, health and the child's parents
Local authority children's social care, the school and the GP
Local authority children's social care, police and health
2.w: Working Together 2026 states that a strategy discussion involving local authority children's social care, the police and health (and other bodies as appropriate, such as the referring agency and education) should take place whenever there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm.

n.0: The LADO manages allegations against people who work with children; children's social care must be involved here.
n.1: Parents are not participants in a professionals' strategy discussion, and the police are required.
n.2: Schools and GPs may contribute, but the police must be involved as a minimum.

2.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
2.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

2.q: Daniel is a registered nurse on a gynaecology ward. He holds a religious objection to abortion and is allocated to help prepare a patient for a surgical termination of pregnancy this afternoon. Under the Code, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell the nurse in charge at the end of the shift that he objects to this work
Tell colleagues, manager and patient, and arrange a qualified colleague to cover
Take part in today's procedure and register his objection with the NMC afterwards
Explain his religious reasons to the patient so that she understands his decision
2.w: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care about a conscientious objection and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over responsibility for that person's care. Section 4(1) Abortion Act 1967 gives the statutory right to refuse to participate.

n.0: Telling one person after the event leaves the patient's care unplanned; Code 4.4 requires colleagues, manager and patient to be told and cover arranged.
n.2: The NMC does not hold a register of objections; Code 4.4 requires him to declare the objection and hand over care in advance.
n.3: Code 20.7 says not to express personal beliefs to people in an inappropriate way; he must tell her he objects, not argue his beliefs.

2.q: Kai, 7 weeks, is in cardiac arrest on a children's ward. Two nurses trained in paediatric life support are giving CPR while the arrest team is on the way. According to RCUK 2025, which chest compression technique should be used for Kai?
o: Two thumbs side by side on the upper third of the sternum
Two fingertips placed on the lower half of the sternum
The heel of one hand placed on the lower half of the sternum
Two thumbs on the lower sternum with hands encircling the chest
2.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support recommends the two-thumb encircling technique for ALL infant compressions (single or two rescuers), on the lower half of the sternum, depth at least one third of the chest, 100-120 per minute.

n.0: Compressions are delivered over the lower half of the sternum; the upper sternum does not compress the heart effectively.
n.1: The two-finger technique was used for lone rescuers in earlier guidance; RCUK 2025 uses two-thumb encircling for every infant.
n.2: One hand (or two) is the technique for a child over 1 year, not for a 7-week-old infant.

2.q: Margaret, 81, has metastatic lung cancer and is being cared for on a medical ward. The team agree she may be in the last days of life and start an individualised care plan. A newly qualified nurse asks how often Margaret should be formally reviewed for changes. Which minimum interval does NICE NG31 recommend for monitoring and updating her care plan?
o: At least every 24 hours
At least every 12 hours
At each weekly multidisciplinary meeting
At least every 72 hours
2.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.6: monitor for further changes in the person at least every 24 hours and update the care plan. Improvement can occur (rec 1.1.3), so regular review guards against wrongly assuming the person is dying.

n.1: Twelve hours is the NG31 minimum for monitoring a person on clinically assisted hydration (rec 1.4.9), not the general review of a dying person.
n.2: A weekly review would miss rapid changes in the last days of life; NG31 asks for monitoring at least every 24 hours.
n.3: Seventy-two hours is too long; NG31 rec 1.1.6 sets a minimum of every 24 hours because the person's condition can change quickly.

2.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
2.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

2.q: Sam, a community nurse, has just given a subcutaneous injection of enoxaparin to Mrs Ada Kowalski, 69, in her home using a prefilled syringe with a safety device. What is the safest way to deal with the used syringe?
o: Separate the needle from the syringe and place each part in the correct waste stream
Place the used syringe in a rigid tray and dispose of it in the sharps bin in the car
Activate the safety device and place the needle and syringe as one unit in the sharps bin at once
Recap the needle with a one-handed scoop technique and dispose of it at the next clinic visit
2.w: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and the National IPC Manual require safer sharps to be used as designed, no recapping, and disposal at the point of use by the user, with the needle and syringe discarded as one unit into a sharps container (FACTS S-HSE, S-NIPCM).

n.0: Needles must not be disassembled from syringes; the unit is discarded intact.
n.1: Carrying an exposed used sharp away from the point of use increases the risk of injury; a portable sharps container should be taken to the point of use.
n.3: Recapping is a recognised cause of needlestick injury and is prohibited by the Sharps Regulations; carrying a recapped needle to another visit adds further risk.

2.q: Kerry, a healthcare assistant, injures her back while helping a patient who began to fall. She is unable to do her normal work for ten days. The ward manager is preparing the RIDDOR report as the responsible person. Within what timescale must the report be made?
o: Within 10 days of the incident
Within 15 days of the incident
Within 7 days of the incident
Within 15 days of her return to work
2.w: Under RIDDOR 2013 an injury that incapacitates a worker for more than seven consecutive days (not counting the day of the accident but including weekends and rest days) must be reported within 15 days of the accident (HSE, RIDDOR: when do I report).

n.0: Ten days is the deadline for the written report of a specified injury or death, not for an over-7-day incapacitation.
n.2: Seven days is the length of incapacitation that makes the injury reportable, not the reporting deadline.
n.3: The 15-day period runs from the date of the accident, not from the worker's return to work.

2.q: Mr Kim, 71, takes bisoprolol for heart failure. He has pneumonia and his respiratory rate is 24, but his heart rate is 74 bpm. A student nurse says his normal pulse shows he is not seriously unwell. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: His normal pulse means a sepsis screen is not needed today
Heart rate is the most reliable sign of infection in older adults
Bisoprolol tends to raise the pulse, so 74 bpm is a low reading
Beta-blockers can blunt the heart rate rise with infection
2.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.4: interpret heart rate in context; older people may not develop an increased heart rate, and the response may be affected by medicines such as beta-blockers. His raised respiratory rate still needs scoring and escalation as appropriate.

n.0: A pulse in the normal range does not exclude sepsis in someone taking a beta-blocker.
n.1: NG253 warns that older people may not show a rise in heart rate, so it is not the most reliable sign.
n.2: Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker that slows the heart rate; it does not raise it.

2.q: A nurse enters the bay of Gladys, 84, to tidy her over-bed table and move her water jug within reach. Gladys is asleep and the nurse does not touch her. The nurse then turns to leave the bed space. Which of the five moments for hand hygiene applies now?
o: After a body fluid exposure risk in the bed space
Before a clean or aseptic procedure on the ward
After touching a patient's immediate surroundings
After touching a patient during a care episode
2.w: The five moments in NIPCM ch 1.2 are before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching a patient's immediate surroundings. Handling the over-bed table and jug is contact with the immediate surroundings, which can be contaminated.

n.0: No blood or body fluid exposure risk occurred while tidying the table.
n.1: The nurse is leaving, not about to start a clean or aseptic task.
n.3: The nurse did not touch Gladys, so the moment 'after touching a patient' does not describe this contact.

2.q: Michael, 61, had a stroke three months ago. He now attends community physiotherapy and speech and language therapy to regain function and adjust to living with weakness in his right arm. Which level of prevention does this care represent?
o: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Population prevention
Secondary prevention
2.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: tertiary prevention is the application of measures to reduce or eliminate long-term impairments and disabilities, minimising suffering from existing ill health and promoting the person's adjustment to their condition.

n.1: Primary prevention aims to stop the disease occurring at all; Michael has already had a stroke.
n.2: This is a population-wide strategy, not care to reduce one person's long-term impairment.
n.3: Secondary prevention detects disease early in people without symptoms, for example through screening.

2.q: Mrs Holt, 80, has advanced dementia and limited speech. During a wash she grimaces, guards her left hip and pulls away when touched there. She cannot say whether she is in pain. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
o: As refusal of care, so the wash should be abandoned
As non-verbal signs of physical distress that need assessment
As features of her dementia that need no further action from staff
As agitation that should be treated with a sedative
2.w: Annexe B 1.2.2 requires nurses to recognise symptoms and signs of physical distress. In people who cannot report pain, behaviours such as grimacing, guarding and withdrawal may indicate pain, so the hip should be assessed further (for example injury from a fall) using an appropriate observational tool.

n.0: Stopping the wash does not address the possible cause of her distress.
n.2: Attributing new behaviour to dementia risks missing a treatable cause such as a fracture.
n.3: Sedation masks the signs and does not treat the underlying cause; assessment comes first.

2.q: During induction, a healthcare support worker asks Femi, a staff nurse, when the standard infection control precautions (SICPs) used on the ward should be applied. Which reply from Femi is accurate?
o: To patients having invasive procedures or with invasive devices
To patients with a known or suspected infection or colonisation
To all patients at all times, whether or not infection is known
To patients with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or an unexplained rash
2.w: NIPCM ch 1 states SICPs are to be used by all staff, in all care settings, at all times, for all patients whether infection is known to be present or not. They reduce transmission from recognised and unrecognised sources.

n.0: Invasive procedures need aseptic technique, but SICPs apply to every patient whether or not a device is present.
n.1: Known or suspected infection triggers transmission-based precautions in addition to SICPs; SICPs themselves apply to everyone.
n.3: These symptoms flag a cross-infection risk for placement decisions, but SICPs are not limited to symptomatic patients.

2.q: In a GP practice, Jamal, a registered nursing associate, is asked to give influenza vaccines at a Saturday clinic. The registered nurses give the vaccine under a patient group direction (PGD). How can Jamal lawfully administer the vaccine?
o: Under a patient specific direction from a prescriber
Under the practice's homely remedy protocol for vaccines
Under the PGD, after signing it as a named practitioner
Under the PGD, while a registered nurse supervises him
2.w: MHRA guidance lists the registered professions that may supply or administer under a PGD (including nurses, midwives, paramedics and pharmacists); nursing associates are not on the list. A nursing associate can administer against a prescription or a patient specific direction from a prescriber.

n.1: Homely remedy protocols apply to non-prescription medicines; influenza vaccine is a POM.
n.2: Signing a PGD does not authorise a profession that the legislation does not include.
n.3: Supervision does not extend PGD use to a profession that is not authorised to use PGDs.

2.q: Grace was born at 30 weeks' gestation and is now 6 months old by her date of birth. Her mother is upset that Grace cannot sit yet when her friend's baby of the same age can. How should the nurse assess Grace's development?
o: Use her corrected age, about 3.5 months, until she is 2 years old
Use her corrected age until she is 6 months old, then use her actual age
Use her age from birth until she starts school, then switch to corrected age
Use her actual age of 6 months because prematurity has no effect on milestones
2.w: For babies born prematurely, developmental age is calculated from the original due date (corrected age) until the child is 2 years old (NHS, baby health and development reviews). Grace was born 10 weeks early, so at 6 months she has a corrected age of about 3.5 months, when independent sitting is not yet expected.

n.1: Correction does not stop at 6 months; it continues until 2 years of age.
n.2: Corrected age is used up to 2 years, not until school entry, and should be used now rather than later.
n.3: Prematurity does affect expected milestones, which is why correction is used for the first 2 years.

2.q: A children's nurse refers Kayla, 3, to children's social care after she attends with linear burns on her back that her mother cannot explain. The social worker says enquiries will begin under section 47 of the Children Act 1989. Which test triggers the local authority's duty to make these enquiries?
o: Parental agreement that an assessment of the family is needed
Proof on the balance of probabilities that harm has occurred
Reasonable cause to suspect significant harm, actual or likely
A police decision that a criminal offence has been committed
2.w: Section 47 of the Children Act 1989 requires the local authority to make enquiries where it has reasonable cause to suspect that a child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm. Unexplained burns in a 3-year-old meet that test.

n.0: Section 47 enquiries are a statutory duty and do not depend on parental agreement, unlike a voluntary s17 assessment.
n.1: Proof on the balance of probabilities is the standard a court applies to facts in care proceedings, not the trigger for s47 enquiries.
n.3: Police may investigate in parallel, but s47 enquiries do not wait for a decision that a crime has occurred.

2.q: During a home visit, a community children's nurse trained in paediatric basic life support finds Ivy, 4 months, unresponsive in her cot and not breathing normally. Her mother has called 999 on speaker phone. The nurse has opened Ivy's airway in a neutral position. What should the nurse do next?
o: Feel for a brachial pulse for up to 30 seconds before acting
Start chest compressions at a ratio of 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Give 5 initial rescue breaths covering Ivy's mouth and nose
Give 2 rescue breaths and then 30 chest compressions
2.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: after opening the airway and confirming absent or abnormal breathing (no more than 10 seconds), give 5 initial rescue breaths, mouth-to-mouth-and-nose in an infant, before starting compressions at 15:2.

n.0: Pulse palpation is unreliable and delays CPR; RCUK limits the check for breathing or signs of life to no more than 10 seconds.
n.1: Compressions at 15:2 follow the 5 initial rescue breaths; children usually arrest from hypoxia, so oxygenation comes first.
n.3: Two breaths then 30 compressions is the adult sequence; RCUK 2025 starts paediatric CPR with 5 rescue breaths.

2.q: Jamal, 4, has cerebral palsy and complex feeding needs. His parents tell the community children's nurse they are exhausted and ask whether the local authority can assess the family for short breaks and practical support. How is Jamal best described under the Children Act 1989?
o: A looked-after child accommodated under section 20
A child in need under section 17 because he is disabled
A child subject to a supervision order under section 31
A child at risk of significant harm under section 47
2.w: Section 17(10) of the Children Act 1989 defines a child in need as one unlikely to achieve a reasonable standard of health or development without services, whose health or development is likely to be significantly impaired without services, or who is disabled. The local authority has a duty to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in need.

n.0: Section 20 accommodation means the child is looked after away from home; Jamal lives with his parents.
n.2: A supervision order under s31 is made by a court when the significant harm threshold is met, which is not the situation described.
n.3: Section 47 enquiries need reasonable cause to suspect significant harm; nothing here suggests harm, only unmet need.

2.q: Ahmed, 72, has end-stage COPD and is on a respiratory ward. He is thought to be in his last days. He tells the nurse he wants to die at home, and his wife says she wants this too and can stay with him. What should the nurse do first?
o: Explain that moving him home in the last days of life is not safe for him
Ask the GP to decide whether a home death would be appropriate
Start arranging the equipment, care and medicines needed at home without delay
Record his wish and review it at next week's multidisciplinary team meeting
2.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.3.4 and 1.3.5: establish as early as possible the resources needed (equipment, care at night, support) and create an individualised care plan that includes the person's preferred care setting. Priority for Care 5: an individual plan of care agreed and delivered with compassion.

n.0: NG31 supports a preferred care setting where possible; transfer is not ruled out simply because he is dying.
n.1: The plan is made with Ahmed, his wife and the multidisciplinary team; deferring the decision to the GP delays action on his wish.
n.3: Waiting a week risks him dying before his wish can be met; NG31 rec 1.3.4 says establish resources as early as possible.

2.q: Elaine, 45, tells the practice nurse she bought a small pack of paracetamol from a supermarket, but the pharmacy said her prescribed codeine needed a prescription. She asks which legal category allows sale from premises such as supermarkets. Which category is correct?
o: Prescription only medicine (POM)
Controlled drug in Schedule 5
Pharmacy medicine (P)
General sale list medicine (GSL)
2.w: MHRA guidance on medicine categories: GSL medicines can be sold from a wider range of premises, such as supermarkets, if the premises can be closed to exclude the public and the medicines are pre-packed. POM and P medicines are sold or supplied from a registered pharmacy, POMs against a prescription.

n.0: POMs need a prescription and are supplied through a pharmacy or other authorised route.
n.1: Schedule 5 is a controlled drug schedule, not a sale category; such products are sold through pharmacies.
n.2: Pharmacy medicines are sold under a pharmacist's supervision at registered pharmacy premises.

2.q: Frank, 70, says he cannot sleep on the ward because of noise and lights. He is not in pain. Which intervention should be tried first?
o: Move his evening medicines to midnight so that he wakes less
Request a hypnotic medicine for him to take every night
Encourage him to nap during the day to make up for lost sleep
Reduce noise and light at night and offer an eye mask and earplugs
2.w: Annexe B 3.6: support rest and sleep with non-pharmacological measures first, such as a quiet, dark environment, eye masks and earplugs, and a routine. Hypnotics carry risks, including falls in older people.

n.0: Moving medicines to midnight adds a night-time disturbance and may be clinically inappropriate.
n.1: Hypnotics are not first line and increase falls and confusion in older people.
n.2: Daytime napping can worsen night-time insomnia.

2.q: Mr Rahman, 58, is a practising Muslim admitted for a planned operation in England. He asks the nurse whether he can be helped to pray at the set times each day and have a quiet space to do so. Which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 most directly protects this request?
o: Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
2.w: Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including manifesting religion in worship and practice. Supporting Mr Rahman to pray is a direct application (HRA 1998 Sch 1).

n.1: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights; it does not itself create the right to practise religion.
n.2: Article 5 concerns liberty and detention, not religious observance.
n.3: Article 8 protects private and family life; religious practice is protected more directly by Article 9.

2.q: Ayesha brings her son Zain, aged 9 months, to a health visitor review. She is worried because Zain picks up small pieces of food with his whole hand in a raking movement and cannot yet pick up a raisin between his thumb and index finger. He sits without support and babbles. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer Zain to a paediatrician for assessment of delayed fine motor development
Arrange a hearing test because fine motor delay often accompanies hearing loss
Explain that a raking grasp is expected now and a pincer grip follows
Advise Ayesha to stop finger foods until Zain develops a pincer grip
2.w: Fine motor skills develop in sequence: a palmar or raking grasp comes first and a fine pincer grip (thumb and index finger) typically appears around 12 months (CDC 2022 milestones list a raking grasp at 9 months and the pincer grip at 1 year). Zain is following the expected sequence, so reassurance and explanation is appropriate (P3.1: applying knowledge of human development).

n.0: Referral is not indicated: a raking grasp at 9 months is within the expected sequence, so there is no delay to assess.
n.1: There is no hearing concern: Zain babbles, and fine motor skills are not used to screen hearing.
n.3: Finger foods help develop grasp and self-feeding; stopping them would remove practice and is not advised.

2.q: A student nurse on a children's ward asks about the order in which gross motor skills usually develop in the first 18 months. Which sequence is correct?
o: Holds head up, sits without support, pulls to stand, walks independently
Sits without support, holds head up, cruises around furniture, walks independently
Rolls over, cruises around furniture, sits without support, walks independently
Holds head up, pulls to stand, sits without support, walks independently
2.w: Gross motor development proceeds head to toe (cephalocaudal): head control (around 2 months), sitting without support (around 9 months), pulling to stand and cruising (around 12 months), then walking independently (by 18 months) (CDC 2022 milestones; T2 child development).

n.1: Head control is the first gross motor milestone and comes before sitting.
n.2: Cruising needs trunk control from sitting, so it comes after, not before, independent sitting.
n.3: Pulling to stand requires the trunk control gained from sitting, so sitting comes first.

2.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse, arrives for a shift on a surgical ward wearing a long-sleeved cardigan, a wristwatch, a plain metal wedding band and short, unvarnished nails. Before giving direct care, which change does she need to make to meet standard infection control precautions?
o: Remove the cardigan, the watch and the wedding band before patient contact
Keep the cardigan on and swap the wristwatch for a fob watch
Remove the cardigan and the watch and keep the plain wedding band on
Roll the cardigan sleeves to the elbow and wear gloves over the band
2.w: NIPCM ch 1.2: before hand hygiene staff must be bare below the elbows and remove hand and wrist jewellery, with the exception of a single plain metal ring, which should be moved during hand hygiene. Short nails without products are already compliant.

n.0: A single plain metal ring is permitted under NIPCM, so the wedding band does not have to come off.
n.1: Long sleeves stop her being bare below the elbows, so keeping the cardigan on is not compliant even with a fob watch.
n.3: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene, and a pushed-up cardigan is not the bare-below-the-elbows standard.

2.q: Peter, 68, is two days after bowel surgery. A healthcare support worker reports that he is 'not himself'. You find him drowsy, with snoring respirations and his tongue falling back. Using the ABCDE approach, what is your first action?
o: Open his airway with a head tilt and chin lift and call for help
Check his capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Review his fluid balance chart and wound drain output
Record a full set of observations and calculate his NEWS2 score
2.w: The ABCDE approach (RCUK) deals with problems in order and treats each one as it is found. Snoring with a falling tongue is partial airway obstruction, which kills fastest, so open the airway with simple manoeuvres and call for help before moving on. Code 15 and P4.10 require a prompt response to deterioration.

n.1: Glucose is checked under D (disability); airway obstruction comes first in the sequence.
n.2: Fluid balance belongs to C (circulation) and does not address the immediate airway threat.
n.3: A full set of observations is useful but delays treating an obstructed airway, which must be dealt with first.

2.q: Edna, 79, has metastatic breast cancer and has capacity. The team believe she is entering the last days of life. Her son meets the nurse in the corridor and asks that Edna is not told she is dying because 'it will crush her'. What is the nurse's most appropriate next step?
o: Tell Edna her full prognosis straight away so she is fully informed
Find out from Edna how much she would like to know about her condition
Agree with her son and avoid discussing the prognosis with Edna
Ask the consultant to decide whether Edna should be told she is dying
2.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.3: establish how much information the dying person would like about their prognosis, then discuss it with them unless they do not wish to be informed, including those important to them if the person wishes. Priorities for Care (2014): sensitive communication and involving the dying person in decisions.

n.0: This ignores her own preference about how much she wants to know; NG31 rec 1.2.1 asks staff to establish this first.
n.2: Edna has capacity and a right to information; NG31 rec 1.2.3 says discuss the prognosis with her unless she does not wish to be informed.
n.3: The decision about how much information she receives rests with Edna, not with a clinician or relative acting for her.

2.q: On Monday morning a children's nurse in England telephones and then confirms in writing a referral to children's social care about Leah, 4, who has unexplained bruising. Leah's mother asks how soon she will hear what happens next. Under Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026, when should social care decide on next steps?
o: Within one working day of receiving the referral
Within 3 working days of the referral
Within 24 hours of the written confirmation arriving
Within 5 working days of receiving the referral
2.w: Working Together 2026 (para 167) states that within one working day of a referral being received, local authority children's social care should decide on next steps, such as no further action, Family Help or s47 enquiries, and inform the referrer.

n.1: Three working days is not the Working Together decision timescale.
n.2: The timescale is expressed in working days from receipt of the referral, not hours from written confirmation.
n.3: Five working days is the timescale for notifying a serious incident to the national panel, not for a referral decision.

2.q: A children's nurse is checking Kofi, 3 days old, for jaundice. Kofi has dark brown skin and the ward lighting is dim. Which approach does NICE CG98 recommend?
o: Check the colour of his palms and soles under the ward lights
Rely on his mother's report, as jaundice is hard to see on his skin
Use an icterometer held against his nose to grade the jaundice
Look at sclerae, gums and blanched skin in bright natural light
2.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023): check the naked baby in bright and preferably natural light, examine the sclerae and gums and press lightly on the skin to look for jaundice in blanched skin. Do not use an icterometer.

n.0: Dim ward light and palms and soles alone miss jaundice; CG98 specifies bright natural light, sclerae, gums and blanched skin.
n.1: Jaundice can be detected on darker skin using sclerae, gums and blanched skin; parental report alone is unsafe.
n.2: CG98 says do not use an icterometer to measure bilirubin.

2.q: Mr Bell, 76, tells the nurse he is 'fine' after hip surgery, but he is grimacing, gripping the bed rail and avoiding eye contact. What is the most appropriate response?
o: "Many people say that after surgery. I'll check on you in an hour."
"You say you're fine, but you look uncomfortable. Can you tell me more?"
"Are you sure? Shall I fetch you some painkillers to be safe?"
"That's good to hear. Let me know if anything changes later on."
2.w: Annexe A 1.1: actively listen, recognise and respond to verbal and non-verbal cues. Code 2.6: recognise when people are anxious or in distress and respond compassionately.

n.0: This dismisses the cues and delays assessment of possible pain.
n.2: Offering analgesia without assessment skips exploring what he is experiencing.
n.3: This accepts the verbal message and misses the non-verbal cues of pain.

2.q: A first-year student nurse asks Tom, her practice supervisor, what the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires of her personally as an employee on the ward. Which statement by Tom is correct?
o: You must ensure the health, safety and welfare of all staff on the ward so far as reasonably practicable
You must report every injury you sustain at work directly to the Health and Safety Executive yourself
You must write a formal risk assessment before carrying out each care task that involves any risk to you
You must take reasonable care of yourself and others affected by what you do, and cooperate with your employer
2.w: Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places two duties on every employee: to take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of other people who may be affected by their acts or omissions, and to cooperate with the employer so that the employer can meet its own duties (FACTS S-HSE).

n.0: Ensuring the health, safety and welfare of employees so far as reasonably practicable is the employer's general duty (s2), not the individual employee's duty.
n.1: RIDDOR reports are made by the responsible person (usually the employer); the employee reports the injury through the local incident system.
n.2: Formal risk assessment is an employer duty under the management regulations; employees follow the assessments and safe systems of work their employer provides.

2.q: Grace, 79, is found by her daughter on the ward to be confused and difficult to rouse. You have assessed and managed her airway, breathing and circulation. Under D (disability), which assessment should you complete?
o: Level of consciousness using ACVPU, pupils and capillary blood glucose
Respiratory rate, chest expansion and oxygen saturation
Pulse, blood pressure and urine output over the last hour
Skin inspection for rashes, pressure damage, wound leakage and drains
2.w: D in the ABCDE approach assesses neurological status: level of consciousness (ACVPU, which NEWS2 uses), pupils and a capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of reduced consciousness.

n.1: Respiratory rate, expansion and saturation belong to B (breathing).
n.2: Pulse, BP and urine output belong to C (circulation).
n.3: Skin, rashes and wounds are examined under E (exposure).

2.q: Priya, a registered nurse on a care of older people ward, is preparing to hoist Alan Hughes, 78, from bed to chair. While checking the sling she notices that one of the seams is frayed and partly torn. Two healthcare assistants are waiting to help. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Transfer Mr Hughes by lifting him with the two healthcare assistants instead of using the hoist
Reinforce the torn seam with strong tape and complete the transfer with the hoist as planned
Use the sling for this transfer with an extra person present, then report the damage afterwards
Withdraw the sling from use, label it as faulty, report it and fetch a suitable replacement
2.w: Faulty lifting equipment must be taken out of use and reported so that nobody else uses it, and the planned safe system of work (hoist with an intact sling) should continue with a replacement. This applies the employee duty under s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 to take reasonable care for others, LOLER 1998 (equipment for lifting people must be safe) and Code 19 (preserve safety).

n.0: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require hazardous manual handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable; a manual lift of a hoist-dependent person replaces one hazard with another.
n.1: Improvised repairs to lifting equipment are unsafe and conceal the defect; damaged slings must be withdrawn and replaced, not patched.
n.2: An extra person does not make a torn sling safe; using it exposes Mr Hughes to a fall and delays reporting a known hazard.

2.q: Tomasz, 17, is admitted to a children's ward in England after a fall from scaffolding at work. A student nurse suggests that, because he is employed full time and lives with his partner, the Children Act 1989 no longer applies to him. How should the nurse respond?
o: The Act applies, because it defines a child as a person under 18
The Act does not apply, because it defines a child as a person under 16
The Act applies, because it covers young people up to their 21st birthday
The Act does not apply, because full-time work ends his status as a child
2.w: Section 105 of the Children Act 1989 defines a child as a person under the age of 18. Working Together 2026 adds that a 16 or 17-year-old living independently, working or in hospital keeps the same status and entitlement to protection.

n.1: 16 is the age for consent under FLRA 1969 s8 and for most of the MCA 2005, not the Children Act definition of a child.
n.2: Some leaving-care duties extend into the early twenties, but the Act's definition of a child stops at 18.
n.3: Employment or independent living does not change a young person's status as a child under s105.

2.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward, is reading the Code during her preceptorship. She wants to know which of the four themes contains the standard on keeping clear and accurate records. Which theme is it?
o: Promote professionalism and trust
Prioritise people
Practise effectively
Preserve safety
2.w: The Code (NMC 2015, updated 2018) has four themes: Prioritise people (1-5), Practise effectively (6-12), Preserve safety (13-19) and Promote professionalism and trust (20-25). Standard 10, keep clear and accurate records, sits under Practise effectively.

n.0: Promote professionalism and trust covers standards 20-25 (reputation, registration, investigations, complaints, leadership), not record keeping.
n.1: Prioritise people covers standards 1-5 (dignity, preferences, needs, best interests, confidentiality); records sit under standard 10.
n.3: Preserve safety covers standards 13-19 (competence, candour, emergencies, raising concerns, medicines, harm reduction); records are standard 10.
